summary: The note celebrates bards as living keepers of history who preserve culture through oral chronicles, using examples of performers at festivals across Scotland, Ireland, West Africa, England and online. It argues that bards convey emotion, educate younger generations, bind communities and are finding new life through digital media and a resurgence of rural folk festivals.
one_line: Bards and oral storytellers preserve history, educate, and unite communities, remaining relevant through folk festivals and digital platforms in the modern age.
key_facts: The annual Folklore Festival brings a small village to life on September 5th, 2023.
Alistair McCrae, a Scottish lore-master, performed on October 9th, 2023 at the Dunbar Folk Festival, telling tales of warriors, lovers and mystical creatures of the highlands.
Myrna O'Hara, an Irish sean-nós singer, entranced her audience on November 12th, 2023 at the Galway Storytelling Festival.
Abubakar Ndoye, a West African griot, performed on December 1st, 2023 at the Senegal Storytelling Summit, threading the lineage of kings through spoken word.
Abubakar Ndoye's performance helped his community understand their ancestry and societal structure, showing the bard as an educator.
Emily Hart's voice at the Somerset Winter Tales Evening on January 7th, 2024 helped bind an intimate English country community.
Amir Sulaiman and Sarah Kay performed spoken word at the Digital Bard Fest, streamed globally on February 15th, 2024.
The Heartland Bardic Roundtable took place on March 20th, 2024, letting traditional storytelling enthusiasts exchange knowledge.
Rural community festivals are seeing a resurgence of interest in bardic art, driven by nostalgia and a yearning for connection in an age of information overload.
The note describes bards as a 'living library' that preserves culture without needing written words.
